title: Announcing First Principles: Rare conversations with the pioneers behind key computing technologies - a16z crypto
gist: a16z crypto announces 'First Principles,' an interview series with the Turing/Nobel/Gödel Prize-winning pioneers of distributed systems, market design, and cryptography, framed around the thesis that crypto's hardest problems are decades-old CS/economics problems now resurfacing in blockchains.

themes.theme: Crypto's hard problems are old CS/econ problems in new clothes

insights.claim: Crypto's hardest problems — decentralized coordination, verification, incentives, adversarial behavior, and trust — are deep systems problems rooted in decades of computer science and economics research, not novel inventions of the blockchain era.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating crypto protocol design should look for teams that draw on established distributed-systems/mechanism-design theory rather than treating consensus, incentive, and verification problems as greenfield.
insights.locator: the broader idea behind First Principles

insights.claim: The popular narrative that the Bitcoin whitepaper appeared out of nowhere in 2009 as a singular breakthrough is a myth — its core ideas were built on distributed-systems, cryptography, and market-design 'first principles' developed decades earlier.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Framing device useful for diligence narratives: trace a protocol's claimed innovation back to its actual academic lineage rather than accepting founder mythology at face value.
insights.quote: People often tell the story of the first Bitcoin whitepaper as if it were a holy relic that appeared out of nowhere in 2009
insights.locator: People often tell the story of the first Bitcoin whitepaper

insights.claim: Host Tim Roughgarden's framing thesis for the series is that getting the basic definitions and abstractions of a technology exactly right allows them to resurface and prove useful many generations of technology later, in ways their original inventors could not have foreseen.
insights.speaker: Tim Roughgarden
insights.so_what: A useful lens for evaluating foundational protocol/primitive work today: durable abstractions (not flashy applications) are what compound in value over decades.
insights.quote: it will inevitably surface (and resurface) many generations of technology later, in ways the pioneers could never have foreseen
insights.locator: If you get it just right

insights.claim: Leslie Lamport's foundational work — including the Byzantine Generals Problem applied to mission-critical coordination systems for NASA, plus causality, logical clocks, safety/liveness, and replicated state machines — forms much of the theoretical basis for blockchain consensus mechanisms.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Consensus-protocol due diligence should be benchmarked against these decades-old formal properties (safety, liveness, Byzantine fault tolerance) rather than novel marketing claims.
insights.locator: Leslie Lamport (most recently at Microsoft Research)

insights.claim: Barbara Liskov's Turing Award-winning work on data abstraction, fault tolerance, and distributed computing underpins practical and theoretical foundations still used in system and programming-language design today.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Fault-tolerance and data-abstraction principles from the 1970s-80s remain the baseline standard against which distributed blockchain infrastructure should be judged.
insights.locator: Barbara Liskov (MIT) won the Turing Award in 2008

themes.theme: Market and auction design as blockchain infrastructure

insights.claim: Paul Milgrom's Nobel-winning auction theory and new auction formats underpin many online marketplaces and protocols today, and were previously applied to design major real-world auctions including radio spectrum auctions conducted by the FCC.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Protocols relying on on-chain auctions (MEV, NFT mints, token sales) are implementing decades-old auction theory — evaluate their mechanism choices against Milgrom-era formats rather than as novel design.
insights.locator: Paul Milgrom (Stanford University) won the Nobel Prize in 2020

insights.claim: Alvin Roth's Nobel-winning theory of stable allocations and market design demonstrated empirically how markets function in practice, not just in theory, through lab experiments and real-world market design.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Market-design theory (stable matching, empirical validation) is directly relevant to designing functioning on-chain marketplaces and matching systems.

themes.theme: Cryptographic primitives that power crypto today

insights.claim: RSA public-key cryptography, co-invented by Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir, and Len Adleman, relies on the fact that no efficient algorithm exists yet for factoring very large integers, and remains critical to secure data transmission systems used broadly today.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: The security assumption behind RSA (factoring hardness) is a specific, falsifiable computational bet — worth tracking against advances in factoring algorithms or quantum computing that could break it.
insights.quote: nobody has yet developed an efficient algorithm for factoring very large integers

insights.claim: Shafi Goldwasser's Turing Award-winning work laid the complexity-theoretic foundations for cryptography and pioneered interactive proof systems, which underpin zero-knowledge systems and SNARKs used across blockchains and other industries today.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Zero-knowledge/SNARK-based scaling and privacy infrastructure (rollups, private transactions) traces directly to Goldwasser's interactive proof theory — a strong signal of the field's academic depth and durability.
insights.locator: Shafi Goldwasser (MIT) won the Turing Award in 2012

insights.claim: Noam Nisan, with Amir Ronen, coined the term 'algorithmic mechanism design,' combining economics and game theory with computer science techniques to analyze how selfish behavior by users and service providers affects complex computational systems like the internet.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Algorithmic mechanism design is the direct academic lineage of token-incentive and protocol-game-theory design work in crypto — a useful framework for evaluating whether a protocol's incentive structure is adversarially robust.
insights.locator: Noam Nisan (Hebrew University of Jerusalem, also Starkware)

themes.theme: Roughgarden's own applied frameworks for crypto economics

insights.claim: Tim Roughgarden authored a framework called LVR (loss-versus-rebalancing) to help liquidity providers decide whether and when to provide liquidity to an automated market maker, addressing a core open question in decentralized finance.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: LVR is a directly actionable analytical tool for LPs and AMM designers to quantify the cost of providing liquidity versus simply holding/rebalancing — relevant to evaluating AMM protocol economics and LP yield claims.

insights.claim: Roughgarden has separately published an analysis of Ethereum's transaction fee mechanism design, applying his game-theory and mechanism-design expertise directly to a live blockchain protocol.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Signals that academic mechanism-design analysis of Ethereum's fee market (e.g., EIP-1559-style design) exists and is treated as serious reference material by a16z crypto's own research lab.
insights.locator: his paper analyzing Ethereum's transaction fee mechanism design
